newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France runs into flak over Thomson.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France runs into flak over Thomson.

text.p: The French government came under fire on Thursday over its suspension of a sale of state-owned electronics giant Thomson SA, with French media accusing it of amateurism and South Korea angrily demanding an explanation.

The government, which had agreed to allow part of the group to be sold to Korean firm Daewoo despite a storm of employee protest and political opposition, made a U-turn after an independent French commission challenged Daewoo's involvement.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe's government has vowed to go forward with the sale but has not yet specified new terms.
South Korea's government on Thursday demanded an "understandable explanation" for the decision amid public allegations there that racism was at least partly responsible.
The Seoul foreign ministry said it had issued a cable through its Paris embassy seeking clarification.
"We have requested an understandable explanation from the French government for our public," a Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
"We would like to know whether the commission's opinion was based on economic factors or public opposition," he said.
The French Foreign Ministry had no immediate comment.
French media branded the suspension a "disaster" and a "fiasco" handled with execrable public presentation and said France's image would be seriously damaged by the debacle.
"This reads like a bad politico-financial thriller," influential financial daily Les Echos said.
Under the shelved privatisation plan, France was to have sold loss-making Thomson to private electronics group Lagardere for a symbolic one franc.
Lagardere planned to sell part of Thomson, television set and video recorder maker Thomson Multimedia, to Korea's Daewoo Electronics -- also for just one franc.
The government said on Wednesday the privatisation commission had not approved of part of the Daewoo spin-off plan and thus the privatisation had to be suspended.
In its confidential report, obtained by Reuters, the commission said the Daewoo deal did not fully reflect the value of Thomson's technology in digital decoders and flat screens.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, said on Thursday he hoped the privatisation of Thomson would take place before the spring and did not rule out breaking up the company in the sale.
"It must be done as quickly as possible," Arthuis said in a radio interview. "I hope it will be done before the spring."
He did not refer to Seoul's demands for explanation.
But he said the government had been in favour of the sale of Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo because it promised to create jobs and rescue the company from its financial distress.
"The government rallied to this idea because Daewoo was in a position to create jobs and dig Thomson out of its ditch," Arthuis said.
Daewoo has repeatedly promised to create as many as 5,000 jobs and invest more than $1.0 billion in France after taking over Thomson Multimedia.

Relations with fast-expanding South Korea have important economic implications for France, which would like a share of Seoul's $24 billion plan to buy or build fighter jets and other other potentially lucrative defence orders.
France's privately owned Dassault Aviation is up against U.S. and other competition to sell its Rafale warplanes.
South Korea is also a rare foreign showcase for French high-speed-train technology and nuclear power stations.
